[quote=western_view;60110362][spoiler=Expansion pt 2]High in a quiet valley of the Pantgruel Mountains, Patragruel Town had stood for centuriesa small Armaralan village where timber artisans crafted their wares and mountain herders tended to their flocks amid the changing seasons.
When Western View began building New Valmoriany nearby, Patragruel Town remained untouched, a haven of tradition surrounded by sweeping change.

Nine-year-old Uilia Voshin had lived with her father in Patragruel Town since her mothers passing. Her mother had fallen ill during their voyage from Western View and died before they could fully settle into Armaralo, leaving Uilia and her father to find strength in each other.

One cold winter day, the earth trembled with a fearsome roar as the avalanche unleashed its fury down the mountainside. Snow and ice crushed everything in its path.
Uilia was inside their small wooden home when the first waves of snow slammed into the village.
Swept from her bed by the avalanches force, she was tossed into a swirling chaos of snow and debris.

Remembering the mountain lore her father had taught her, Uilia instinctively grabbed onto an overturned wooden table that had been thrown from the house.
She pressed beneath it, creating an air pocketenough to keep her breathing as snow buried her alive.
For what felt like hours, Uilia lay in silence, holding her breath, the cold pressing in but the air trapped beneath the table sustaining her.

Days later, Hans Dartiduf, a skilled skier exploring the slopes near the disaster site, noticed a faint tapping sound beneath the snow.
Digging carefully, rescue workers uncovered Uilia, weak and cold but alive.
Hans stayed by her side, wrapping her in warm blankets, his calm presence a lifeline in the overwhelming silence.

Taken to Valmira for treatment, Uilia faced not only recovery from her injuries but the loss of her home and fatherwho, tragically, had been unable to escape the avalanche.
Despite the grief, Uilias resilience shone through. She learned to walk again, to speak of her experiences, and slowly to hope.

Though Patragruel Town vanished beneath the snow and time, Uilia carried its memory in her heart.
She became a quiet symbol of survival and courage, sharing her story with others and reminding the world of the human lives beneath the mountains and ambitions. But the mountains werent the only dangerous place in Armaralo.
The sky above New Wessernia had been deceptively calm for most of the day. Settlers went about their routines, busy with construction projects and daily life in the bustling coastal settlement. The sharp tang of the sea breeze mixed with the scent of fresh timber and earth, masking the brewing storm far out over the Nestor Ocean.

Meteorological technology, while advanced, had failed to provide sufficient warning. The hurricane had formed rapidly, its path unpredictable, catching the settlementand its peopleoff guard.

That evening, dark clouds roared in from the ocean, whipping winds into a frenzy. Rain fell in sheets, flooding streets and undermining hastily built shelters.
As the hurricanes eye passed directly over New Wessernia, the storm unleashed its full fury: torrential rains, winds exceeding 150 miles per hour, and towering waves crashing against the shoreline.

The settlement, built quickly to accommodate the pressing expansion, lacked the reinforced infrastructure to withstand such a tempest. Buildings crumbled, power lines snapped, and emergency services struggled to respond amid the chaos.

More than 10,000 people lost their lives in the stormfamilies, workers, childrencaught in the destruction.

In the days that followed, rescue operations began amid the wreckage. Survivors huddled in makeshift shelters, grieving lost loved ones and grappling with the fragile hope of rebuilding.

Head Council Mack Messiaon addressed the nation with a heavy heart: Our people have endured an unimaginable tragedy. We must honor the fallen by rebuilding stronger, smarter, and with greater respect for the forces we face.

The hurricane was another painful reminder that even in a modern world, natures power could overwhelm human ambitionand that expansion came with both opportunity and risk.
The morning after the hurricane, New Wessernia lay in ruins. Streets were flooded and strewn with debristorn roofs, shattered glass, overturned vehicles, and fallen trees. The once-bustling port was eerily silent, save for the distant cries of survivors and the rumble of rescue helicopters.

Emergency teams from across Western View and Armaralo mobilized swiftly. The Wessernian Coast Guard dispatched boats to reach flooded neighborhoods, while medical personnel set up triage centers in the few standing buildings.
Volunteerssettlers and locals alikeworked side by side, digging through rubble to find survivors. Makeshift shelters sprang up in cleared areas, offering food, warmth, and a place to grieve.

[i]Jalen Meris[/i], now a young teenager, had been at school when the storm hit. His classrooms sturdy construction saved many lives, but Jalen still lost two close friends that day. He spent hours helping teachers comfort younger students, his hands trembling as he passed out blankets and water.
[i]Amira Selen[/i] coordinated logistics for rescue teams. Her experience managing infrastructure projects became invaluableshe helped prioritize areas needing power restoration and secure temporary water supplies.
[i]Lina Vash[/i], though miles away in Valmira, organized volunteers to send care packages and staffed a crisis hotline for distraught families seeking news.

Despite the devastation, the spirit of New Wessernias people remained unbroken. Stories of heroism emerged: neighbors pulling each other from flooded homes, strangers sharing what little food they had, and rescue dogs sniffing through wreckage to find survivors.

Back in Wessernias Council chamber, the hurricanes impact sparked fierce debate.
Councilor Varrin Kehl called for a comprehensive review of New Wessernias construction standards. We rushed this settlement without proper safeguards. This tragedy is a direct consequence.
Councilor Mara Den countered, We must rebuild quickly. Our people need hope and jobs. Delays will only deepen suffering.
Head Council Mack Messiaon sought a middle path. We owe it to the victims to rebuild strongerwith better planning, modern engineering, and early warning systems. But we cannot let fear stall our progress.

The Council passed emergency legislation to:
[*]Fund advanced meteorological stations across the Nestor Ocean for improved hurricane tracking.

[*]Enforce stricter building codes designed to withstand severe weather.

[*]Establish a disaster response task force integrating Wessern and Armaralan resources.

[*]Launch public education campaigns on storm preparedness.

The hurricane also intensified dialogue with Armaralos government, which offered aid and support. While some settlers worried about over-reliance on local assistance, others saw cooperation as essential to survival.

As New Wessernia slowly rose from the wreckage, its scars were a somber testament to the delicate balance between human ambition and natures mighta balance that Western View would have to navigate carefully in its expansion eastward.

In the weeks following the hurricanes devastation, frustration simmered among the people of New Wessernia and back home in Wessernia. Many blamed the governments rushed expansion policies and inadequate disaster preparedness for the tragedy that had cost over a thousand lives.

In New Wessernia, crowds gathered daily at the central plaza, their voices rising in anger and grief. Signs called for accountability, better safety measures, and a halt to expansion until the settlement could be made safe.
Simultaneously, in Wessernias capital city, protesters marched through the streets outside the Council chamber. Citizens demanded transparency, justice for victims families, and a reevaluation of Head Council Mack Messiaons leadership.

Amid the tension, extremist groups seized the moment. One faction called for a complete withdrawal from Armaralo, seeing the expansion as a colonial overreach. Another blamed local Armaralans, stoking ethnic hatred.

Hatzur Zatsugi, an infamous international terrorist born in Western View but radicalized abroad, saw the unrest as an opportunity to deepen division. His network had long exploited political fractures worldwide.
Unbeknownst to authorities, Zatsugis operatives infiltrated protest crowds in both New Wessernia and Wessernia, armed and ready to incite chaos.

On a tense afternoon, during a massive protest in Wessernias central square, shots rang out.
Panic erupted as gunfire tore through the crowd. Dozens were wounded; several died in the chaos.
The assailants fled into the maze of streets, their identities initially unknown but later traced to Zatsugis extremist cells.

Head Council Mack Messiaon addressed the nation, condemning the violence and vowing swift justice.
Security forces increased patrols and tightened controls on public gatherings.

The shooting shocked the world and brought fresh scrutiny to Western Views internal security and its complicated expansion into Armaralo.
Allies urged cooperation to root out extremist networks, while critics demanded a halt to what they called a reckless expansion fueling instability.

The shadow of Hatzur Zatsugi and the tragic shooting marked a dark chapter in Western Views storya stark reminder of the fragile line between progress and peril.
In the wake of unrest and tragedy, Head Council Mack Messiaon recognized that healing divisions required more than words from afar. With the national election looming, he announced a historic visit to Armaralothe first by a Western View leader since expansion began.

Messiaons goals were clear but complex:
[*]Rebuild trust with Armaralan communities shaken by recent events.

[*]Show solidarity with the settlers and locals affected by disasters and unrest.

[*]Present his vision for a stable, cooperative future between Western View and Armaralo.

[*]Gather support among the growing population of settlers and sympathetic Armaralans ahead of the election.

Messiaon arrived in Valmira amid tight security and a wary crowd. His convoy passed through streets still bearing scars from recent conflicts and natural disasters.
He met with local leadersincluding Lina Vash and other community representativesto listen firsthand to concerns about safety, cultural preservation, and cooperation.

At public forums and town halls, Messiaon emphasized shared futures and mutual respect.
We are bound by more than land, he declared. We are bound by our hopes, our families, and the challenges we face together.

Not all received him warmly. Protesters voiced distrust, questioning whether his promises would translate into action.
The opposition used his visit to criticize what they called a political stunt amid ongoing crises.

Back in Wessernia and New Wessernia, media coverage of the trip sparked debate. Supporters praised Messiaons courage and willingness to engage directly. Critics argued for stronger reforms before elections.

Messiaon planned follow-up visits, policy proposals, and coalition-building efforts to solidify his standing.
His journey to Armaralo became a defining momentan attempt to bridge divides in a nation navigating the difficult path between expansion and unity.

Head Council Mack Messiaon had planned to travel to Armaralo aboard his private jet, a symbol of his status and efficiency. But just hours before departure, mechanical issues grounded the aircraft for urgent repairs.

With the election clock ticking, Messiaon had no choice but to book a commercial flight. The airline initially scheduled him on Flight 472, departing late morningjust enough time to reach Armaralo for his planned meetings.
He arrived at the airport with his security detail, prepared for the journey.

However, moments before boarding, the airline announced a delay. Flight 472 was rescheduled for the late afternoon due to technical checks on the plane.
Though frustrated, Messiaon changed his flight to flight 1012.

Hours later, news broke that Flight 472 had vanished over the ocean shortly after takeoff. The plane, carrying 264 passengers and crew, was nowhere to be found.
Search and rescue teams scrambled, but as the night deepened, hope waned.

Messiaon sat stunned in the airport, the narrow escape weighing heavily on him.
This delay it saved my life, he confided to a trusted aide. But so many others lost.

The tragedy dominated headlines, overshadowing Messiaons political mission.
Questions arose about airline safety, emergency preparedness, and fates cruel hand.

Despite the shock, Messiaon resolved to honor those lost by redoubling efforts to bring stability and safety to Western View and Armaralo. But more disasters followed.
The ground beneath Armaralo shuddered violently, the earths deep rumble shaking buildings and shattering windows across the region. At 3:17 PM local time, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck along the Pantgruel-Shamat Fault Line, sending shockwaves through the coastal towns of Westmore, Jolhslandia, and Zaasasa.

Though the quakes violent shaking lasted less than two minutes, its destruction was immense. Seventeen people were confirmed dead from collapsed structures and falling debris in the affected towns. Many more were injured, with emergency services stretched thin as aftershocks rattled nerves and buildings.

Worse was yet to come.
Minutes after the quake, the ocean surged. A massive tsunamiwaves towering over thirty feet highrushed toward the coast, sweeping through the low-lying areas with unstoppable force.
The towns of New Valmoriany and Gratenburg, built along the shoreline and still recovering from previous disasters, bore the brunt of the tsunamis fury.

Entire neighborhoods were submerged or swept away. Roads vanished beneath water, and rescue crews faced impossible conditions navigating flooded streets and damaged infrastructure.
Casualties mounted quickly245 confirmed dead, with 92 still missing and feared lost beneath the waves.

Rescue operations launched immediately, with teams from Western View and Armaralo coordinating to search for survivors, clear debris, and provide aid.
Temporary shelters filled quickly, while medical facilities struggled to cope with the influx of injured.
Head Council Mack Messiaon, addressing the nation, expressed grief and solidarity: We mourn those lost in this terrible tragedy. Our commitment is to rebuild stronger and safer, and to stand united with all who have been affected.

The disaster renewed calls for improved infrastructure, early warning systems, and emergency preparednessespecially in the earthquake-prone fault zone.
The Grand Assembly Hall in Wessernia was packed. Citizens, council members, and representatives from all corners of Western View had gathered to hear Head Council Mack Messiaons response to the growing public outcry.
Protests demanding an end to the expansion had erupted across the nationtoo many lives lost, too much destruction, people cried. The earthquake, the tsunami, the hurricane, the shootingsall weighed heavily on the peoples hearts and minds.

After many called for a cancellation of the Armaralo expansion, Mack Messiaon made a speech, standing at the podium, Mack Messiaons voice was steady, his eyes sweeping across the crowd.
My fellow Wesserns, he began, I hear your pain. The losses we have sufferedat New Wessernia, New Valmoriany, and beyondare wounds that will take time to heal. But I ask you to listen, not just with your hearts, but with the wisdom of our history.

[b]Our story begins long before Western View was called Western View.[/b]
Before colonialism, this land was known as Valmorniany, home to two great peoplesthe Wesserns and the Valmornians. The Valmornians once held sway, but the winds of history shifted with the arrival of Eastornia-Kolionia. This sparked the Valmorniany Wars, a long and bitter struggle.
Mistrust and division tore us apart then. The Wesserns, though once allies of the Kolionians, rose to claim our own destiny. We remember the pain of those timesthe fighting, the bloodshed, the fragile peace won at great cost.

[b]In the 18th century, Eastornia-Kolionias civil war left us taxed and torn, our people impoverished.[/b]
We watched as our Valmornian brothers and sisters suffered injustice, and in the 19th century, that pain erupted in revolutiona fight for dignity, independence, and hope.

[b]The 20th century saw us rise from division to unitythough not without struggle.[/b]
Wesserns declared independence in 1923, asserting democracy and self-rule. Though the Valmornian government resisted, by 1932, Western View was bornan island nation standing proud.

[b]We discovered oil in 1933, a blessing and a curse, as the Great Oil Fire taught us hard lessons on safety and resilience.[/b]

[b]Through the cold shadows of nuclear proliferation, Western View chose a different pathpeace, democracy, and law.[/b]
We formed alliances with neighbors, founded IPEA, and sought a future where cooperation prevailed over conflict.

[b]But darkness still lurks. The terror wrought by Hatzur Zatsugi reminds us of the fragility of peace.[/b]
He was born here, among us, yet turned away from all we stand for. We must remain vigilant.

[b]And now, faced with loss and hardship, you ask why expansion must continue?[/b]
Because Western View is more than an island. It is a people growing fast, bursting at the seams of our beloved homeland. Our island holds 100 million souls, but space and resources are finite.
We must reach beyond our shoresto Armaraloto build a future where our children breathe freely, where our industries thrive, and where our democracy grows stronger.

[b]This is not a reckless ambition. It is a continuation of our historya story of survival, of resilience, and of hope.[/b]
We honor those lost by building safer cities, stronger communities, and by listening to all voicesWessern and Armaralan alike.

[b]Let us not be paralyzed by fear but inspired by the courage of those who came before us.[/b]
Together, we will forge a future worthy of Western Views proud legacy.

Mack Messiaon stepped back from the podium to a room filled with thoughtful silence. Then, slowly, applause begantentative at first, then growing.
The path ahead remained difficult, but the spirit of Western View was unbroken.

It had taken [b]four years.[/b]
Four years since the Category 5 hurricane tore through the coastal jewel of New Wessernia, flattening buildings, flooding streets, and killing over a thousand souls in the space of a few horrific hours. What had once been a vibrant seaside hub of commerce and culture was reduced to a shattered, salt-soaked wasteland.
But now, on a warm spring morning, the air was filled not with the stench of decay, but with the mingled aromas of [b]fresh paint, blossoming coastal flowers, and sea breeze[/b].

The reconstruction had not been easy.
The initial months were chaosrelief camps, disease outbreaks, protests about the governments slow response. Then came the [b]Rebuild New Wessernia Initiative[/b], an ambitious publicprivate partnership funded partly by Western Views federal government, partly by IPEA disaster aid, and partly by the grit of its own surviving citizens.
Roads were repaved with [b]storm-resistant materials[/b], and all new structures were [b]elevated on reinforced platforms[/b] to survive future storm surges. The once low-lying harbor was rebuilt with a [b]tsunami-resistant seawall[/b] stretching the entire waterfront.
Whole neighborhoods were reimaginednot just rebuilt, but redesigned for resilience. Underground power lines replaced the old pole system. Drainage canals doubled as green parkways. Emergency shelters were embedded into community centers and schools.

At the citys heart stood the [b]Hurricane Dawn Memorial[/b], a sleek crescent-shaped wall of polished stone engraved with the names of the dead. In the center was a bronze sculpture: a child holding a lantern toward the sea.
Visitors left flowers at its base every week. Survivors still wept there. And childrentoo young to remember the hurricaneasked their parents why the lantern pointed toward the horizon.

Once the physical rebuilding neared completion, the city turned to economic revival. The government offered [b]five-year tax incentives[/b] for small businesses willing to reopen in New Wessernia. Tourismonce deadslowly trickled back, drawn by stories of a city that refused to drown.
A state-of-the-art [b]offshore wind farm[/b] was built nearby, giving New Wessernia clean energy and hundreds of jobs. The portWestern Views third-largestwas expanded with deeper channels and automated cargo handling, attracting new trade routes.

On the day of completion, the entire central promenade was draped in blue-and-white banners, the colors of Western Views coastal provinces. A stage faced the harbor, and thousands gathered to watch.
Head Council Mack Messiaon stood alongside Mayor Clara Revens, cutting the ribbon that officially declared New Wessernia rebuilt, renewed, and ready.
Cheers erupted, and fireworks burst over the seawall. Ships in the harbor blasted their horns in salute.

But even in celebration, there was quiet acknowledgment[b]the citys scars would never fully fade[/b]. For many, the new streets and shining towers were not just signs of progress, but reminders of what was lost.

Long before the glass towers, neon streets, and bustling ports of modern Armaralo, the northern frontier was a place few dared to tread. It was dense with [b]ancient cedar forests[/b], carved by rivers that twisted like silver threads, and shadowed by mountains that seemed to hold their own secrets.
One of those secrets was the story of [b]Aren Tavan[/b], a man whose name had faded into the footnotes of Western Views history books.

Aren had been a surveyor, cartographer, and self-taught naturalistdrawn to the unexplored by an insatiable curiosity. In 1964, he set off from Eastern Harbor with a small pack, a compass, and a rifle, bound for the upper reaches of the Armaralo Peninsula. He told his young wife, [b]Elda Tavan[/b], that he would be back before the next frost.
He never returned.
Despite a three-month search by local authorities and volunteers, no sign of him was ever foundno camp, no supplies, no body. People assumed he had been swept away by one of Armaralos sudden flash floods, or perhaps mauled by a bear in the thick woods. Elda refused to believe he was dead, but eventually, even she had to let go.

Sixty-one years later, as construction crews began clearing land for the expansion of [b]New Western View[/b], a team widening an old logging road in the upper Armaralo ranges spotted smoke rising from a grove of pines.
Curious, they hiked in.
What they found was something out of a different centurya small log cabin, weathered but sturdy, with hand-carved shutters and a stone chimney puffing thin trails of woodsmoke into the morning air.
And on the porch sat [b]Aren Tavan[/b].

His beard was long and silver. His eyes, though wrinkled at the corners, were startlingly bright.
Hed never left. After getting lost in a snowstorm in the winter of 64, he had stumbled upon this spot, built a shelter, and stayedhunting, fishing, growing vegetables in the short summers.
I figured the world would come find me if it wanted to, he told the astonished workers. Looks like it finally did.
When asked why he never tried to make it back, Aren only smiled faintly. I had everything I needed here. Except her.
Inside the cabin, above the neatly kept hearth, was a small black-and-white photograph of a young woman smiling in the sun.
It was [b]Elda Tavan[/b].

The story spread quicklyan explorer thought dead for six decades, found alive in the wilderness. The government offered him a home in the city, but he refused. He agreed only to visit for a few weeks, staying in New Western View long enough to see the ocean again, taste fresh bread, and marvel at how much the world had changed.
He stood at the waterfront one evening, watching the sunset burn the horizon orange, the wind from the harbor tugging at his worn coat.
Shes gone, I know, he said to a local reporter. But if shes somewhere up there, I hope she knows I never stopped thinking of her.
When the visit ended, Aren returned to his cabin in Armaralo, leaving behind a signed map of the forests he called home. In one corner, in spidery handwriting, were the words:
For Elda. I found my wayjust not the way we planned.

The last two years had altered Western View more than the last fifty.
 It had not been a gradual change, but a series of sharp fracturesnatural disasters hitting like hammer blows, political tempests tearing through institutions, and tragedies striking in places thought untouchable.
Avalanches had erased villages. Hurricanes had wiped coastlines nearly clean. Earthquakes had rattled the Pantragruel-Shamat fault line, and the sea had risen in vengeance to swallow towns whole. Terrorists had turned protests into massacres, and the nations leaders had been forced to walk a knife-edge between ambition and public grief.
And yetdespite the enormity of what had been lostthere was persistence.

The coastal skyline of [b]New Wessernia[/b] now glittered at night, a city reborn from the wreckage. The streets were wider than before, built with reinforced concrete and elevated above the old flood line. Memorials to the more than 1,000 who died in the hurricane stood in the city squaressimple walls of stone, each name carved deep enough to last centuries.
In the harbors, fishing boats bobbed again, though the fishermen spoke quietly of those who had never returned. The smell of salt and grilled seafood drifted through the rebuilt market, where children played between the stalls as if there had never been a storm.
It was, to outsiders, a miracle of urban renewal. To locals, it was still a woundbut one they had learned to live with.

High in the mountains, [b]Patragruel Town[/b] was being rebuilt not for its economic value, but because of a single name: [b]Uilia Voshin[/b].
The girl who had survived the avalanchetrapped under the snow, saved by the air pocket she had made under a tablewas now something of a national figure. At ten years old, she was shy in public, always clutching her fathers hand during interviews. But she had begun to speak at mountain safety workshops, telling schoolchildren how to find air when the snow comes down.
Snow is heavy, she once told a crowd in Western Views capital. But you can still make space if you know how. Its like the mountains are testing you.
Her father, weathered and quiet, rarely spoke at these events. But when the cameras werent rolling, he would sometimes whisper to her, Your mother would be proud.

Along the Pantragruel-Shamat fault, the towns of Westmore, Jolhslandia, and Zaasasa had been patched back together, but the sea-facing ruins of [b]New Valmorniania[/b] and [b]Gratenburg[/b] were left as they weresalt-streaked skeletons of buildings standing half-submerged in the shallows.
Visitors sometimes wandered there at low tide, picking their way over broken boardwalks. Some swore the silence there felt different, heavier. As if the sea waasstill remembered.

Then came the story of [b]Aren Vostren[/b], the explorer who had vanished into Armaralos wilderness sixty-one years ago.
His quiet reemergence stunned the nation. He had been presumed dead decades earlieranother name in the long catalog of Western Views explorers lost to storms, crevasses, and isolation. Instead, he had been living in a weathered cedar cabin, heating it with a stone fireplace, trapping game, and planting a narrow garden on the slope.
His beard was snow-white, his hands calloused, his eyes startlingly sharp for a man in his eighties. When asked why he had stayed, he simply said, I knew the world would still be there if I ever came back. I wasnt sure the mountains would be.

In the capital, journalists treated him like a celebrity. Children lined up to shake his hand. He was offered honorary citizenship, a state pension, even a seat on an exploratory advisory board. But he declined them all.
Ive been alone too long to start living in cities, he told Mack Messiaon himself in a brief meeting. But Ill visit. Sometimes.
Before he left, he showed reporters a single possession he had kept safe through blizzards, lean winters, and the long quiet of mountain lifea faded photograph of his wife, [b]Elda Tavan[/b]. She had died before his disappearance, and he had carried her image in a leather pouch ever since.
I didnt make it back to her, he said. But I carried her with me everywhere I went. I think maybe thats what we all docarry the ones we lose, and try to keep building something worth showing them if we ever meet again.

When Aren returned to his cabin, he went on foot, walking the forest trails alone. But he wasnt going back to a world completely untouched by the cityhe had promised to leave a carved signpost at the edge of his property, pointing toward the nearest settlement, for the next lost soul.
And so, as the capital buzzed with the noise of politics, as New Wessernias cranes swung steel into place, and as Uilia Voshin learned to climb higher into the alpine passes, the smoke from Aren Vostrens chimney curled into the sky.
The world moved on.
But in the deep cedar forests of Armaralo, one man still kept his own quiet watchover the mountains, over the memories, and over the unbroken thread of Western Views story.
[b]Final Speech of Head Council Mack Messiaon[/b]
[i](Delivered to the People of Western View and Armaralo, Winter 2027)[/i]
[b]My friends my family my fellow Wesserns[/b]
We have walked through a fire that few nations have endured and remained whole. In just a handful of years, our island home and our new lands in Armaralo have been tested beyond measure.
We have seen the mountains themselves move, bringing snow down upon our villages. We have seen the ocean rise in anger, sweeping away our coastal towns. We have felt the wind of hurricanes tear at our very doors, and we have heard the crack of the earth along the Pantragruel-Shamat Fault Line.
And we have mourned.
We have mourned the thousands lostfrom the 1,000 souls of New Wessernia to the 245 who perished in the tsunami, to those who vanished without warning on Flight 638, to the innocent lives stolen by the cruelty of terror.
But this is also a day to remember the living.
[b]Elda Tavan[/b], who in her later years reminded us that wisdom can guide policy as firmly as ambition.
[b]Ravi Koothar[/b], whose skill in engineering turned plans on paper into the steel and stone of cities, even when the ground beneath them trembled.
[b]Amira Selen[/b], whose work in New Valmoriany brought hopeuntil tragedy struck, and yet whose legacy still powers the lights of our winter nights.
And the youngest among us[b]Uilia Voshin[/b], who survived the avalanche of Patragruel Town and turned her survival into a lesson that has already saved lives. She taught us that even under crushing weight, we can still carve out the space to breathe.
I speak too of [b]Hans Dartiduf[/b], who refused to ski past danger and instead brought a child back from the ice. Of the rescuers in the hurricanes aftermath, who went into flooded streets when the storm had barely passed. Of the builders of New Wessernia, who turned rubble into towers.
And finally, of [b]Aren Tavan[/b]the man who vanished into the wilderness sixty-one years ago, not to die, but to live, and who has now returned with stories of solitude, strength, and the wife he still carries in his heart.
These are our heroesnot because they were fearless, but because they were human.
We are a small nation, but we have proven that small nations can rise from great trials. We are an island people who now live on two shores. We are a democracy that has stayed standing even when the storms came from every direction.
